s01: Welcome. I am Akṣapāda, a name tradition gives to Gautama, the author of the Nyāya-sūtra. The text has five adhyāyas, each in two āhnikas: ten parts. This edition counts five hundred thirty-three sūtras; other editions differ a little. Tap any part of the map, and let us begin.
s02: The very first sūtra promises a result: from true knowledge of sixteen topics, the highest good. The second sūtra says how. Pain depends on birth, birth on activity, activity on fault, and fault on false cognition. Remove the root, and each link falls in turn, ending in release. Try breaking the chain.
s03: Sūtra one, one, one is a single long compound naming sixteen padārthas, the topics of study: from pramāṇa, the means of knowing, to nigrahasthāna, the grounds of defeat in debate. For now, sort the sixteen into four families. This grouping is a study aid, not the sūtra's own.
s04: Four pramāṇas, says sūtra one, one, three: perception, inference, analogy and testimony. Perception is cognition born of contact between sense and object, not tied to a word, not erring, and determinate. Read that sūtra word by word, then decide which pramāṇa gives each piece of knowledge.
s05: Sūtra one, one, five says inference follows perception, and is threefold. Pūrvavat moves from a seen cause to its effect, like clouds to rain. Śeṣavat moves from a seen effect back to its cause, like a muddy river to rain upstream. Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa works from general likeness. Commentators read these differently, so take these as classic illustrations.
s06: Next come the twelve prameyas, the things worth knowing: self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, fault, rebirth, fruit, pain and release. The self is known by its marks: desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition. Tap each to read its sūtra, then test yourself.
s07: How does an inquiry begin? With doubt, saṃśaya: a wavering that wants a distinguishing feature. Then a purpose, an accepted example and tenet, an argument, tarka, and finally nirṇaya, settled ascertainment. Put the stages in order on the puzzle of a post or a person at dusk.
s08: Now the heart of Nyāya reasoning: five members, the avayavas. Thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion. The example carries the general rule, and it can be positive, by similarity, or negative, by dissimilarity. Arrange the five members of the hill and smoke argument, then switch to the negative example.
s09: Why does the smoke argument work? Wherever there is smoke there is fire: vyāpti, invariable concomitance. But fire does not always bring smoke: a red-hot iron ball shows it. Pick a reason and a target in this little world, and look for the counterexample.
s10: Sūtras one, two, one to three define three kinds of discussion. Vāda seeks truth, with proof, tarka and five members. Jalpa has the same form but also allows chala, jāti and nigrahasthāna. Vitaṇḍā only attacks. Sort six moves into the three.
s11: Sūtra one, two, four lists five faulty reasons, the hetvābhāsas: the deviating, the contradictory, the question-balancing, the one no clearer than what it proves, and the one that comes too late. Later logicians use a slightly different five. Read each argument, and name its defect, or declare it sound.
s12: Chala is a quibble: blocking a statement by imagining a different meaning. Sūtras one, two, ten to fourteen name three kinds. Vākchala plays on wording. Sāmānyacchala over-stretches a general statement. Upacāracchala takes figurative speech literally. Sort these exchanges.
s13: In adhyāya two, Nyāya turns on itself. An objector says no pramāṇa can be established, since it would have to come before, after or together with what it proves. The reply: the objector's denial needs a pramāṇa too, and a pramāṇa can be known as a lamp's light is. Choose the replies.
s14: Adhyāyas three and four argue for the self, and for the way out. One object is both seen and touched, so someone must unite the senses. The mind is inferred because cognitions do not arise at once. Adhyāya four ends by guarding truth, like a thorn fence around young seedlings.
s15: Adhyāya five is the debater's field manual. Twenty-four jātis: futile rejoinders that look like refutations but rest on mere similarity or difference. And twenty-two nigrahasthānas, grounds of defeat, such as abandoning your thesis, or having no reply. Match six losing moves to their names.
s16: Navya-Nyāya, the new Nyāya, is traced to Gaṅgeśa, around the thirteenth or fourteenth century. Scholars like Ingalls and Matilal note its exact language of relations, its focus on cognitions, and its careful handling of absence. Compare it with Aristotle and Dignāga, then build an absence the Navya-Nyāya way.
s17: Now build your own inference. Choose a locus, a reason and a target, and the workbench checks three things: is the reason in the locus, does it pervade the target, and is the target already contradicted. Then take the final quiz. Pass it, and you take the rank of Naiyāyika.
